study.title: 2 Timothy 1 O courage, faithfulness, and the deposit of the gospel
study.overview: Paul opens the letter by remembering that his apostolate comes from the will of God and is linked to the promise of life in Christ Jesus. He greets Timothy with pastoral affection and then thanks God for the constant memory of the disciple in his prayers. The chapter insists that sincere faith should be revived, that the gospel produces courage rather than fear, and that suffering is part of Christian fidelity. Paul anchors everything in the salvation accomplished by Christ, in the incorruptibility of the apostolic message and in the need to keep the good deposit of the teaching received. At the same time, he contrasts the abandonment of many with the loyalty of Onesiphorus, whose practical help and courage are remembered with gratitude.

outline.title: Apostolic Greeting and Life Promise
outline.explanation: Paul presents himself as an apostle by the will of God and relates his mission to the promise of life in Christ Jesus. The greeting to Timothy is warm, asking for grace, mercy and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus the Lord.

outline.title: Gratitude, faith inherited and God-given courage
outline.explanation: Paul prays without ceasing for Timothy, recalls his tears and points out the faith without pretending that he marked his family. With this, it exhorts Timothy to revive the gift received; the foundation of this exhortation is that God does not grant fear, but power, love and self-control.

outline.title: Don't be ashamed, suffer by the gospel, and keep the deposit
outline.explanation: Timothy is called not to be ashamed of the testimony of the Lord or of Paul's chains, but to share in suffering according to the power of God. Paul explains salvation as God's gracious initiative in Christ, now revealed in the manifestation of Jesus, who overcame death. Therefore, the messenger must keep the pattern of sound words and keep the good trustees by the Holy Spirit.

outline.title: Abandonment of Onesíphorus's faithfulness and faithfulness
outline.explanation: Paul reports that many in Roman Asia have abandoned him, which contrasts with Onesyphorus, who comforted him, was not ashamed of his prisons and sought him diligently in Rome. The chapter ends with a prayer for him to find mercy on that day, also recognizing the help he gave in Ephesus.

study.context: The notes provided show that the letter is born in the context of suffering and expectation of persecution, with Paul reminding Timothy of the possibility of suffering for remaining faithful. Tyndale notes that the section from 1:5-14 is an appeal for Timothy to go to Rome without fear; Matthew Henry points out that Paul's greetings and thanksgiving follow a frequent pattern in his letters. It is not necessary to affirm more than this from the notes: the chapter brings an intense personal relationship between Paul and Timothy, and a scenario in which some move away and others remain loyal.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that the so-called Christian does not rely on human merit, but on the will of God and the grace given in Christ Jesus before the times. Salvation appears as a divine initiative that becomes manifest in history by the appearance of Jesus Christ, whose work defeats death and paves the way for life and immortality. It is also clear that the gospel produces an ethics of courage: not fear, but power, love and self-control; not shame, but perseverance in suffering. Faithfulness includes keeping the correct form of the message received and protecting it by the Holy Spirit. At the same time, the text values concrete means of encouragement in the community: prayer, grateful memory, family example of faith, and practical service such as Onesiphorus. In evangelical reading, this holds that Christian perseverance is a gift of God, but requires an obedient and vigilant response from the believer.

scholarViews.insight: The note links the promise of life in Christ to the resurrection of Jesus and shows that this hope responds to the suffering of the godly; the promised life in 1:1 is a central part of the letter's argument.
The exhortation to revive the gift of God is understood as a call to exercise and use the gifts received; the believer needs to be remembered and stimulated in service.

The expression of mercy can be understood as a form of prayer so that, on the great day, Onesiphorus receives mercy from the Lord; Clarke sees there a semitic formula of spiritual blessing and desire.

questions: What fear or shame today prevents me from clearly assuming the testimony of Christ?
How can I revive the gifts and responsibilities that God has already entrusted to me?
Who, in my walk, has been like Onesiphorus: someone who consoles, seeks and does not abandon in difficult times?
study.practice: This week, take time to pray for a specific person as Paul did for Timothy, gratefully remembering the faith that God has already operated on it. Then identify an aspect of your Christian service that needs to be rekindled - Bible study, prayer, witness, service - and practice it intentionally, without letting yourself be guided by fear. If there is suffering or embarrassment because of the gospel, ask the Lord for courage not to be ashamed and also seek to encourage someone who is going through similar pressure.
study.uncertainty: The notes do not safely inform the exact date or the precise place in which the letter was written; it is also not possible to determine, only by this chapter and by these notes, the exact role of Thing and Hermogenes in the church or all the details of the abandonment mentioned. The interpretations of some expressions - such as the prayer for mercy in 1:18 are presented by the commentators as possibilities, not as absolute certainty of the text.
